points.quote: free electrons drop into the nearby holes and leave a thin barrier with nothing free to move
points.problem: One paragraph carries semiconductor, doping, n-type, p-type, holes, source, drain, barrier, oxide, gate and bridge. I had to read it twice to see why the barrier blocks current and how the gate undoes it. The closing sand/oxide sentence also reads as an afterthought.
points.hint: split into two paragraphs: what doping does, then the gate and the barrier

points.quote: can add numbers, hold them and carry out a program like a Turing machine's
points.problem: The step from 'two switches in a row give AND' to 'adding and holding numbers and running programs' is a big jump. 'Hold them' is never pictured.
points.hint: one concrete step between AND and adding, or say plainly that Chapter 2 will show it

points.quote: The first general-purpose electronic computer, ENIAC (1945)
points.problem: A few paragraphs earlier Colossus was 'the first programmable electronic digital computer'. I could not tell how 'general-purpose' differs from 'programmable', or why ENIAC is also called first.
points.hint: say what ENIAC could do that Colossus could not

points.quote: a 3-nanometre process, each smaller than the width of a flu virus
points.problem: 'Process' is not explained. I also could not tell whether 3 nm is the size of one transistor or the name of a manufacturing method.

points.quote: KEY
points.problem: The column of letters on the left is headed only KEY, yet the highlighted blue F is meant to be the lamp. I could not tell keys from lamps in the picture. The small letters above the rotors (B, A, A) are unlabelled, and 'plugboard' in the list is never introduced.
points.hint: label the lamp column and the rotor start letters, or drop the plugboard mention

points.quote: base
points.problem: 'Base' is on the figure before the next section defines it. The caption says a small signal controls a much larger current, but nothing in the picture shows small against large.

points.quote: each gridline is ten times the one below
points.problem: The labelled lines (100, 10 K, 1 M, 100 M, 10 B) are 100 times apart. There are unlabelled lines between them, so the label spacing contradicts the caption and I had to work out which lines count.
points.hint: label every line or say 'every second line is labelled'

points.quote: The red flashes. A tube burning out.
points.problem: I looked at the frames and saw no red anywhere in the ENIAC drawing. I could not connect this list item to anything on screen. The two frames I saw were identical.
points.hint: make the flashes visible, or cut the item

points.quote: main memory became faster much more slowly
points.problem: The sentence reads awkwardly and I had to read it twice. 'Clocks' and 'ticks a second' are used loosely, with no sense of what a tick is.

The figure shows assembly (mov eax, 5) before the next section explains assembly, and 'eax' is unexplained. Why the second instruction sits at 0x05 and not 0x01 is only answered in the list's last step, and fully only in Fig 1.10, which comes after.
points.hint: say in the caption that the first instruction takes 5 bytes

points.quote: then 0x05, then 0x08
points.problem: I had no way to see why the counter jumps from 0 to 5 to 8. The paragraph never says that instructions have different lengths.

points.quote: mov eax, 5
points.problem: 'eax' and 'mov' are not explained here. I took it on trust that this is 'put 5 in a slot', and that was not a real stop.

points.quote: the pipeline must keep fetching before the condition is known
points.problem: I could not see why the condition is not known yet. The idea that it is still being worked out further down the pipeline is missing. The jump from 'out of order' to 'guessing' also felt abrupt.

points.quote: the trace Spectre and Meltdown read
points.problem: Spectre and Meltdown are named here, but the box that explains them comes later and the caption comes first. I did not know what was being read or by whom.
points.hint: 'the trace attacks such as Spectre read (see the box below)'

points.quote: uses it to pick one of 256 memory locations to load
points.problem: This is one long sentence. I could not follow how a secret byte 'picks' a location (the program loads from a place chosen by the byte) or why the fast read reveals it. 'Past a permission check' also comes before the reader knows about permissions.
points.hint: split it into steps: read the byte, load the location it names, time all 256

points.quote: the gold one, a system call, is let through
points.problem: 'System call' appears here as if I knew it. The previous paragraph says only 'ask the kernel', and the term is defined in the next subsection. Why the rings are numbered 3 and 0 is also unexplained.

points.quote: driver
points.problem: The figure labels 'driver' and 'scheduler' inside the kernel, but neither is explained until the list below the figure.

points.quote: waiting
points.problem: The curved dotted line from 'you' down to the CPU block is not explained. I could not tell what it shows, or why I wait until 10:00 when my job ended at 9:40.

points.quote: To the kernel a running program is a process
points.problem: 'Process' is introduced with no setup, and the /proc/1234 example feels like a sudden leap. 'The language it is written in' never names the language.
points.hint: name the language (C) and give process one plain sentence

points.quote: Hiding these gaps is the job of the caches
points.problem: The sentence lists the SSD gap too, but the caches sit between CPU and RAM and do not hide the SSD gap. That is a small mismatch.

points.quote: Peter Denning's working set model (1968) made the idea rigorous
points.problem: The 'working set model' is only a name. I never learned what it says or what 'the idea' is, because locality came several lines earlier. The Part II, III and IV pointers refer to things I have not met.
points.hint: cut the name-drop, or say what the model states in one clause

points.quote: or read a program's file in from disk only as its pages are first used
points.problem: I could not picture this claim. The page-fault explanation then interrupts the list in the middle of 'Flexibility', so 'Protection' arrives after a detour and I had to re-read to keep the three items apart.

points.quote: so the MMU's execute check stops them once DEP marks it not
points.problem: DEP is used before it is defined, and the sentence is hard to parse. Function, buffer, stack and return address arrive in one sentence, with no picture, so I could not see how the extra bytes land on the return address.
points.hint: say what DEP is in four words, and give a small picture or analogy of the overflow

points.quote: 1st read
points.problem: The small white squares in the L1, L2, L3 and RAM bars have no legend. I guessed they are copies of the data but could not confirm it.
